claim: WikiProject Medicine (WPM) maintains articles on Wikipedia about health and medicine.
source: Articles on Wikipedia about health and medicine are maintained by WikiProject Medicine (WPM), and are widely used by health professionals, students and others.
evidence: Directly stated in the abstract of the manuscript.

claim: WPM articles are widely used by health professionals, students and others.
source: Articles on Wikipedia about health and medicine are maintained by WikiProject Medicine (WPM), and are widely used by health professionals, students and others.
evidence: Stated in the abstract without specific data provided in this manuscript, but presented as established fact.

claim: WPM articles are longer than other articles on Wikipedia.
source: We found that WPM articles are longer, possess a greater density of external links, and are visited more often than other articles on Wikipedia.
evidence: Supported by data presented in Table 2 and Figure 1 showing WPM pages average 13,084.9 characters vs 7,676.4 for W pages.

claim: WPM articles possess a greater density of external links than other articles on Wikipedia.
source: We found that WPM articles are longer, possess a greater density of external links, and are visited more often than other articles on Wikipedia.
evidence: Supported by data in Table 2 showing external links appear every 450.3 characters in WPM vs every 657.3 characters in W.

claim: WPM articles are visited more often than other articles on Wikipedia.
source: We found that WPM articles are longer, possess a greater density of external links, and are visited more often than other articles on Wikipedia.
evidence: Supported by data in Table 3 showing WPM pages receive 4.4 times more pageviews per page than W pages.

claim: Readers of WPM articles are more likely to hover over footnotes than other readers.
source: Readers of WPM articles are more likely to hover over and view footnotes than other readers, but are less likely to visit the hyperlinked sources in these footnotes.
evidence: Supported by data in Table 5 showing 120.5 pageviews per hover event for WPM vs 203.5 for W.

claim: Readers of WPM articles are more likely to view footnotes than other readers.
source: Readers of WPM articles are more likely to hover over and view footnotes than other readers, but are less likely to visit the hyperlinked sources in these footnotes.
evidence: Supported by data in Table 5 showing 211.8 pageviews per footnote click for WPM vs 316.3 for W.

claim: Readers of WPM articles are less likely to visit the hyperlinked sources in footnotes than other readers.
source: Readers of WPM articles are more likely to hover over and view footnotes than other readers, but are less likely to visit the hyperlinked sources in these footnotes.
evidence: Supported by data in Table 5 showing 227.6 pageviews per external click for WPM vs 146.7 for W.

claim: WPM readers appear to use links to external sources to verify and authorize Wikipedia content, rather than to examine the sources themselves.
source: Our findings suggest that WPM readers appear to use links to external sources to verify and authorize Wikipedia content, rather than to examine the sources themselves.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the pattern of higher hovering/footnote viewing but lower external clicking observed in the data.

claim: Wikipedia intends to provide every single person on the planet free access to the sum of all human knowledge.
source: Wikipedia is a freely available online encyclopedia that intends to provide "every single person on the planet free access to the sum of all human knowledge" (Wikimedia Foundation, 2004).
evidence: Cited from Wikimedia Foundation, 2004.

claim: Thousands of volunteer editors have created almost six million English-language Wikipedia pages.
source: To meet this mission, thousands of volunteer editors have created almost six million English-language Wikipedia pages.
evidence: Stated as a fact about Wikipedia's scale.

claim: Many Wikipedia pages include hyperlinked footnotes to the sources used to assemble and verify the content.
source: Many of these pages include hyperlinked footnotes to the sources used to assemble and verify the content (Redi et al., 2018; Wikipedia Foundation, 2019a).
evidence: Supported by citations to Redi et al., 2018 and Wikipedia Foundation, 2019a.

claim: Linked references on Wikipedia serve as sources of authority for Wikipedia content.
source: These linked references do not only serve as sources of authority for Wikipedia content (Fallis, 2008), but also offer readers a gateway to further learning, with this opportunity enhanced by the growing degree of public access to research literature (Piwowar et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Fallis, 2008.

claim: Linked references on Wikipedia offer readers a gateway to further learning.
source: These linked references do not only serve as sources of authority for Wikipedia content (Fallis, 2008), but also offer readers a gateway to further learning, with this opportunity enhanced by the growing degree of public access to research literature (Piwowar et al., 2018).
evidence: Stated as a function of linked references, with enhancement noted by citation to Piwowar et al., 2018.

claim: There is a growing degree of public access to research literature.
source: These linked references do not only serve as sources of authority for Wikipedia content (Fallis, 2008), but also offer readers a gateway to further learning, with this opportunity enhanced by the growing degree of public access to research literature (Piwowar et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Piwowar et al., 2018.

claim: Wikipedia is a leading source of health information.
source: Wikipedia is proving to be a leading source of health information (Heilman and West, 2015; Laurent and Vickers, 2009), and reader engagement with a page's references can provide opportunities to understand a diagnosis or inform a conversation with their physician.

claim: Reader engagement with a Wikipedia page's references can provide opportunities to understand a diagnosis or inform a conversation with their physician.
source: Wikipedia is proving to be a leading source of health information (Heilman and West, 2015; Laurent and Vickers, 2009), and reader engagement with a page's references can provide opportunities to understand a diagnosis or inform a conversation with their physician.

claim: Wikipedia's health-focused pages are thought to meet a high standard of quality and rigor.
source: Wikipedia's health-focused pages, which are maintained by WikiProject Medicine (WPM) editors, are thought to meet a high standard of quality and rigor (James, 2016; Maskalyk, 2014; Trevena, 2011).

claim: WPM provides a series of resources for its editors, including guidelines and policies for reliable sources.

claim: WPM recommends using review articles (especially systematic reviews) published in reputable medical journals.

claim: Students and practitioners in medicine and other health-related professions are active Wikipedia readers.

claim: Medical and health professional students and practitioners are familiar with the research literature.

claim: Medical and health professional students and practitioners are expected to engage in evidence-based medicine.

claim: Faculty at several health professions schools teach courses on editing Wikipedia.
source: To this end, faculty at several health professions schools, such as schools of medicine and pharmacy, teach courses on editing Wikipedia (Azzam et al., 2017; Joshi et al., 2019; Apollonio et al., 2018).

claim: A previous study investigated Wikipedia as a gateway to further reading through external links by tracking referrals from Wikipedia to research article DOIs through Crossref.

claim: Previous data could not determine if a click to an external reference with a DOI originated from a WPM page.

claim: Data for this study was collected between March 22nd – April 22nd, 2019 from Wikimedia's Event Logging system and the production MediaWiki database.
source: With the approval and support of the Wikimedia Foundation (WMF), we collected the data presented in this study between March 22nd – April 22nd, 2019 from Wikimedia's Event Logging system and the production MediaWiki database.

claim: The data remained within Wikimedia's system for a year before being deleted.
source: The data remained within that system, as required by WMF, for a year before being deleted (see Acknowledgements).

claim: The aggregated data was anonymized by removing IP addresses, any identifying browser information, and reader-sessions associated with page edits.
source: We anonymized the aggregated data by removing IP addresses, any identifying browser information, and reader-sessions associated with page edits.

claim: The code utilized to collect and analyze the data is organized and made publicly available in a collated series of Jupyter notebooks in GitHub.
source: The code utilized to collect and analyze the data, however, is organized and made publicly available in a collated series of Jupyter notebooks in GitHub (Steinberg and Picardi, 2019; copy archived here).

claim: The data is drawn from English Wikipedia pages in the main namespace.

source: In addition to being able to see at a glance (or a hover) whether the cited work is a review (which is recommend by Wikipedia as being the "ideal source"), readers are able to identify publication date, language, publication venue (i.e., journal name), and availability (via open access) (Figure 3A).
evidence: Stated as Wikipedia's recommendation.

claim: Readers are able to identify publication date, language, publication venue (i.e., journal name), and availability (via open access) from hovering over or viewing citations.
source: In addition to being able to see at a glance (or a hover) whether the cited work is a review (which is recommend by Wikipedia as being the "ideal source"), readers are able to identify publication date, language, publication venue (i.e., journal name), and availability (via open access) (Figure 3A).
evidence: Stated as information available from hovering, illustrated in Figure 3A.

claim: In some instances it is possible to obtain from a citation details on patient populations, medical interventions (e.g., treatments, diagnostic tests), and outcomes involved in the study.
source: In addition, in some instances it is possible to obtain from a citation details on patient populations, medical interventions (e.g., treatments, diagnostic tests), and outcomes involved in the study or whether the source is a standard medical textbook in the field (Figure 3B).
evidence: Stated as information available from citations, illustrated in Figure 3B.

claim: In some instances it is possible to obtain from a citation whether the source is a standard medical textbook in the field.
source: In addition, in some instances it is possible to obtain from a citation details on patient populations, medical interventions (e.g., treatments, diagnostic tests), and outcomes involved in the study or whether the source is a standard medical textbook in the field (Figure 3B).
evidence: Stated as information available from citations, illustrated in Figure 3B.

claim: The greater attention that WPM readers are paying to citations could well be a function of their educational backgrounds, reflecting the demonstrated use of WPM by health professionals, students and practitioners.
source: The greater attention that WPM readers are paying to citations could well be a function of their educational backgrounds, reflecting the demonstrated use of WPM by health professionals, students and practitioners.
evidence: This is an inference connecting the observed behavior to the known user demographics.

claim: The educational value of internal links, in which terms on a WPM page are hyperlinked to other Wikipedia pages or to VideoWiki, should be noted as a further strategy for maintaining the comprehensive informational and educational quality of WPM pages.
source: Although not the focus of this study, the educational value of internal links, in which terms on a WPM page are hyperlinked to other Wikipedia pages or to VideoWiki, should also be noted as a further strategy for maintaining the comprehensive informational and educational quality of WPM pages.
evidence: This is a statement about the educational value of internal links, though not the focus of the study.

claim: One possibility is that readers are deterred from clicking on external WPM links in light of the finding that only a fifth of the research cited in WPM pages are publicly accessible, with the rest placed by publishers behind a paywall.
source: One possibility is that readers are deterred from clicking on external WPM links in light of our finding that only a fifth of the research cited in WPM pages are publicly accessible, with the rest placed by publishers behind a paywall for subscribers or credit card access.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the lower external click rate, based on the data about open access availability.

claim: Only a fifth of the research cited in WPM pages are publicly accessible.
source: One possibility is that readers are deterred from clicking on external WPM links in light of our finding that only a fifth of the research cited in WPM pages are publicly accessible, with the rest placed by publishers behind a paywall for subscribers or credit card access.
evidence: This is consistent with the earlier finding that 22.1% of PubMed citations are labeled as freely accessible.

claim: Earlier studies have found that it is common for readers, including physicians, who encounter a paywall to be reluctant to explore the literature further.
source: Earlier studies have found that it is common for readers, including physicians, who encounter a paywall to be reluctant to explore the literature further (Moorhead et al., 2015; Maggio et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to Moorhead et al., 2015 and Maggio et al., 2016.

claim: If all the research literature was available through open access (and this fact was promoted among readers) health professionals may be more likely to pursue the greater educational advantage of the external links.
source: It is possible that if all the research literature was available through open access (and this fact was promoted among readers) health professionals may be more likely to pursue the greater educational advantage of the external links.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about potential future behavior.

claim: Currently, there are very few links bearing an open access icon.
source: Currently, there are very few links bearing an open access icon, and readers show no additional interest in viewing these links just because they are open.
evidence: This is consistent with the earlier finding that 22.1% of PubMed citations are labeled as freely accessible.

claim: Readers show no additional interest in viewing links with open access icons just because they are open.
source: Currently, there are very few links bearing an open access icon, and readers show no additional interest in viewing these links just because they are open.
evidence: This is based on the earlier finding that there was no evidence of differential clicking on open access links.

claim: If readers start expecting that external links will be open (and there is some promotion of this fact), then the chances of them pursuing an item of interest will become more likely.
source: If readers start expecting that external links will be open (and there is some promotion of this fact), then the two studies just cited suggest that the chances of them pursuing an item of interest will become more likely.
evidence: This is a speculative statement based on inference from cited studies.

claim: This study does not provide a means of determining why readers hover rather than click on external links.
source: Although this study does not provide a means of determining why readers hover rather than click on external links, this is something that could be addressed using smaller-scale research strategies like reader questionnaires or think-aloud protocols.
evidence: Stated as a limitation of the current study.

claim: The question of why readers hover rather than click could be addressed using smaller-scale research strategies like reader questionnaires or think-aloud protocols.
source: Although this study does not provide a means of determining why readers hover rather than click on external links, this is something that could be addressed using smaller-scale research strategies like reader questionnaires or think-aloud protocols.
evidence: This is a suggestion for future research.

claim: Design experiments could be conducted involving WPM pages in which all external links are clearly indicated as open access, tested readers are given prior training in how to learn from cited works, and how different mobile interfaces impact the amount research studies are clicked on for further reading.
source: Alternatively, design experiments, which experiment with external link format and context, could be conducted involving, (a) WPM pages in which all external links are clearly indicated as open access, (b) tested readers are given prior training in how to learn from cited works, and (c) how different mobile interfaces impact the amount research studies are clicked on for further reading.
evidence: This is a suggestion for future research.

claim: One of the limitations of this study is the way in which the count for 'hovering' captures both intentional and unintentional acts.
source: One of the limitations of this study is the way in which the count for "hovering" (defined as a reader's cursor lingering over a link for 1000 milliseconds or more, revealing a rollover label) captures both intentional and unintentional acts.
evidence: Stated as a limitation of the study.

claim: There is no reason to believe that the incidental hovers would differ between WPM and W readers.
source: So, while the reported number of hovers is of limited value, there is no reason to believe that the incidental hovers would differ between WPM and W readers.
evidence: This is a logical inference about the distribution of unintentional hovers.

claim: Various strategies were used to exclude pages visited by bots, but the limited effectiveness of these strategies is a known weakness in Wikipedia's infrastructure.
source: As well, with the pageview data, various strategies were used to exclude pages visited by bots, but the limited effectiveness of these strategies is a known weakness in Wikipedia's infrastructure.
evidence: Stated as a limitation of the data collection.

claim: The exclusion of interwiki links reduced external link counts.
source: This is similarly the case with the exclusion from this study of interwiki links that reduced external link counts, as described in the methods.

claim: This study focuses only on the English-language version of Wikipedia.
source: Lastly, this study focuses only on the English-language version of Wikipedia and therefore our findings are limited to this version of the encyclopedia.

source: The study has identified a number of distinctions that set WPM pages apart from the rest of Wikipedia.

claim: Differences such as page length and link density reflect the quality of WPM pages as information sources.
source: These differences, such as page length and link density, reflect the quality of these pages as information sources.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the observed differences.

claim: Differences in reader behavior, such as time spent on page and amount of external link engagement, support the finding that WPM pages are higher quality information sources.
source: This finding was further supported by differences in reader behavior, such as time spent on page, and amount of external link engagement, particularly the rate readers hover or click on footnote numbers to examine the bibliographic information on the sources contained in the links.
evidence: This is an interpretation connecting reader behavior to page quality.

claim: WPM readers are more engaged in assessing the citation of the external link, which assists in validating and building trust in the content that makes up the WPM pages, than by the opportunity to visit the sources as a gateway for further learning.
source: This suggests that WPM readers are more engaged in assessing the citation of the external link, which assists in validating and building trust in the content that makes up the WPM pages, than by the opportunity to visit the sources as a gateway for further learning.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the observed behavior patterns.

source: Subsequent studies of readers engagement with Wikipedia's external links should investigate the role citations play in what readers learn about a topic and whether there is the potential, especially for readers in health professions, to increase the degree and depth of learning.
evidence: This is a recommendation for future research.

claim: A normality test was used to determine the type of statistical test to apply for time to first engagement with a link and length of the articles.
source: In our analysis, we verified the statistical differences between WPM and W page for the following parameters: (a) time to first engagement with a link, (b) length of the articles, and (c) the number of page loads per event. For parameters (a) and (b) we used a normality test to determine the type of statistical test to apply.
evidence: Stated as a methodological detail.

claim: After rejecting the normality hypothesis, Mann-Whitney U-Test was applied for time to first engagement and article length comparisons.
source: In both comparisons, after rejecting the normality hypothesis, we applied Mann-Whitney U-Test, a non-parametric test that does not require normality assumptions on the two distributions.
evidence: Stated as a methodological detail.

claim: A two-tailed Fisher's exact test was used to compare the two groups over all possible combinations of access method and type of engagement for the number of page loads per event.
source: For the third parameter (c), we compared the two groups over all possible combinations of access method and type of engagement with a two-tailed Fisher's exact test.
evidence: Stated as a methodological detail.
